claim: Translational control by eIF2α bidirectionally regulates auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: Using a combination of behavior, pharmacology, in vivo surface sensing of translation (SUnSET) and DiOlistic labeling we found that, translational control by the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 alpha (eIF2α) bidirectionally regulates auditory but not visual imprinting and related changes in structural plasticity in chickens.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on multiple experimental approaches including behavior, pharmacology, SUnSET, and DiOlistic labeling.

claim: Translational control by eIF2α does not regulate visual imprinting in chickens.
source: Using a combination of behavior, pharmacology, in vivo surface sensing of translation (SUnSET) and DiOlistic labeling we found that, translational control by the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 alpha (eIF2α) bidirectionally regulates auditory but not visual imprinting and related changes in structural plasticity in chickens.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that eIF2α regulates auditory but not visual imprinting based on experimental data.

claim: Increasing phosphorylation of eIF2α reduces translation rates in chickens.
source: Increasing phosphorylation of eIF2α (p-eIF2α) reduces translation rates and spine plasticity, and selectively impairs auditory imprinting.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Increasing phosphorylation of eIF2α reduces spine plasticity in chickens.
source: Increasing phosphorylation of eIF2α (p-eIF2α) reduces translation rates and spine plasticity, and selectively impairs auditory imprinting.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Increasing phosphorylation of eIF2α selectively impairs auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: Increasing phosphorylation of eIF2α (p-eIF2α) reduces translation rates and spine plasticity, and selectively impairs auditory imprinting.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of an eIF2α kinase enhances auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: By contrast, inhibition of an eIF2α kinase or blocking the translational program controlled by p-eIF2α enhances auditory imprinting.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Blocking the translational program controlled by p-eIF2α enhances auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: By contrast, inhibition of an eIF2α kinase or blocking the translational program controlled by p-eIF2α enhances auditory imprinting.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Manipulations of eIF2α-mediated translational control can reopen the critical period for auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: Importantly, these manipulations are able to reopen the critical period.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Imprinting is a form of early learning where exposure to a stimulus becomes the triggering signal of a vital behavior.
source: Imprinting is a form of early learning where exposure to a stimulus becomes the triggering signal of a vital behavior (Jin et al., 2016; Horn, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Jin et al., 2016; Horn, 2004).

claim: Imprinting occurs exclusively within a short critical period.
source: A particular feature of imprinting is that it occurs exclusively within a short critical period (CP) (Jin et al., 2016; Bolhuis, 1991; Nevitt et al., 1994), when structural and functional changes take place (Hensch, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Jin et al., 2016; Bolhuis, 1991; Nevitt et al., 1994; Hensch, 2004).

claim: Structural and functional changes take place during the critical period for imprinting.
source: A particular feature of imprinting is that it occurs exclusively within a short critical period (CP) (Jin et al., 2016; Bolhuis, 1991; Nevitt et al., 1994), when structural and functional changes take place (Hensch, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Hensch, 2004).

claim: Imprinting drives a vigorous following behavior in chickens that is key for filial attachment.
source: Imprinting drives a vigorous following behavior in chickens, key for filial attachment (Horn, 2004; Insel and Young, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Horn, 2004; Insel and Young, 2001).

claim: The formation of imprinted memories has been described across sensory modalities.
source: The formation of imprinted memories has been described across sensory modalities (Nevitt et al., 1994; McCabe et al., 1982; Remy and Hobert, 2005; Bock et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Nevitt et al., 1994; McCabe et al., 1982; Remy and Hobert, 2005; Bock et al., 1997).

claim: In chickens, auditory and visual imprinting relies on different brain structures.
source: Interestingly, in chickens, auditory and visual imprinting relies on different brain structures.
evidence: This statement is supported by subsequent descriptions of the specific brain regions involved.

claim: Imprinted sounds activate the mediorostral nidopallium/mesopallium (MNM) in chickens.
source: Imprinted sounds activate the mediorostral nidopallium/mesopallium (MNM) (Bock and Braun, 1999; Wallhäusser and Scheich, 1987), where neural responsiveness increases after training (Bredenkötter and Braun, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Bock and Braun, 1999; Wallhäusser and Scheich, 1987; Bredenkötter and Braun, 1997).

claim: Neural responsiveness in MNM increases after auditory imprinting training in chickens.
source: Imprinted sounds activate the mediorostral nidopallium/mesopallium (MNM) (Bock and Braun, 1999; Wallhäusser and Scheich, 1987), where neural responsiveness increases after training (Bredenkötter and Braun, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Bredenkötter and Braun, 1997).

claim: The intermediate medial mesopallium (IMM) is required for visual imprinting in chickens.
source: In contrast, the intermediate medial mesopallium (IMM, former IMHV) (Horn, 2004; McCabe et al., 1982) is required for visual imprinting, where neural responses shift to favor the imprinted object (Horn et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Horn, 2004; McCabe et al., 1982).

claim: Neural responses in IMM shift to favor the imprinted object during visual imprinting.
source: In contrast, the intermediate medial mesopallium (IMM, former IMHV) (Horn, 2004; McCabe et al., 1982) is required for visual imprinting, where neural responses shift to favor the imprinted object (Horn et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Horn et al., 2001).

claim: Imprinting requires protein synthesis.
source: While imprinting requires protein synthesis (Gibbs and Lecanuet, 1981), little is known about the underlying translational control mechanisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Gibbs and Lecanuet, 1981).

claim: Translation initiation is believed to be the rate-limiting step in protein synthesis.
source: Translation initiation is believed to be the rate-limiting step and a key target for translational control (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Buffington et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Buffington et al., 2014).

claim: Translation initiation is regulated by modulating the formation of the ternary complex via phosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: A major way in which translation initiation is regulated is by modulating the formation of the ternary complex via phosphorylation of the translation-initiation factor eIF2α.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field of translational control.

claim: In rodents, protein synthesis controlled by phosphorylation of eIF2α is critically required for long-lasting forms of synaptic plasticity.
source: In rodents, protein synthesis controlled by phosphorylation of eIF2α is critically required for long-lasting forms of synaptic plasticity (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2007; Di Prisco et al., 2014) as well as long-term memory storage in several systems (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2007, 2005; Zhu et al., 2011; Stern et al., 2013; Ounallah-Saad et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2007; Di Prisco et al., 2014).

claim: In rodents, protein synthesis controlled by phosphorylation of eIF2α is critically required for long-term memory storage in several systems.
source: In rodents, protein synthesis controlled by phosphorylation of eIF2α is critically required for long-lasting forms of synaptic plasticity (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2007; Di Prisco et al., 2014) as well as long-term memory storage in several systems (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2007, 2005; Zhu et al., 2011; Stern et al., 2013; Ounallah-Saad et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2007, 2005; Zhu et al., 2011; Stern et al., 2013; Ounallah-Saad et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2013).

claim: Chickens showed imprinting to visual cues one day after hatching (P1).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012), chickens showed imprinting to either visual or auditory cues one day after hatching (P1) but not after four days (P4) (Figure 1c and d), indicating that the CP for imprinting ends before P4.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and d, and is consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012).

claim: Chickens showed imprinting to auditory cues one day after hatching (P1).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012), chickens showed imprinting to either visual or auditory cues one day after hatching (P1) but not after four days (P4) (Figure 1c and d), indicating that the CP for imprinting ends before P4.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and d, and is consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012).

claim: Chickens did not show imprinting to visual cues four days after hatching (P4).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012), chickens showed imprinting to either visual or auditory cues one day after hatching (P1) but not after four days (P4) (Figure 1c and d), indicating that the CP for imprinting ends before P4.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and d, and is consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012).

claim: Chickens did not show imprinting to auditory cues four days after hatching (P4).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012), chickens showed imprinting to either visual or auditory cues one day after hatching (P1) but not after four days (P4) (Figure 1c and d), indicating that the CP for imprinting ends before P4.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and d, and is consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012).

claim: The critical period for imprinting in chickens ends before P4.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Yamaguchi et al., 2012), chickens showed imprinting to either visual or auditory cues one day after hatching (P1) but not after four days (P4) (Figure 1c and d), indicating that the CP for imprinting ends before P4.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the experimental data showing imprinting at P1 but not P4.

claim: Imprinting training increased translation in MNM after a 2 hr training session.
source: We found that imprinting training increased translation both in MNM and IMM (Figure 2b,c) after a 2 hr training session, compared to controls, which were running on the wheel but presented with an empty screen.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b,c using the SUnSET protocol.

claim: Imprinting training increased translation in IMM after a 2 hr training session.
source: We found that imprinting training increased translation both in MNM and IMM (Figure 2b,c) after a 2 hr training session, compared to controls, which were running on the wheel but presented with an empty screen.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b,c using the SUnSET protocol.

claim: Two-hour training triggered robust auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: Two-hour (Figure 3a, right panel) training triggered robust auditory imprinting, which was blocked by the protein synthesis inhibitor clycloheximide (CHX) injected immediately after training (Figure 3a, left panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Auditory imprinting triggered by two-hour training was blocked by cycloheximide (CHX) injected immediately after training.
source: Two-hour (Figure 3a, right panel) training triggered robust auditory imprinting, which was blocked by the protein synthesis inhibitor clycloheximide (CHX) injected immediately after training (Figure 3a, left panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: One-hour training did not elicit significant auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: In contrast, one-hour training did not elicit significant auditory imprinting (Figure 3a, right panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: One-hour training triggered visual imprinting in chickens.
source: While one-hour training triggered visual imprinting that was suppressed by CHX (Figure 3b, left panel), visual imprinting after two-hour training was not blocked by post-training administration of CHX (Figure 3b right panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Visual imprinting triggered by one-hour training was suppressed by CHX.
source: While one-hour training triggered visual imprinting that was suppressed by CHX (Figure 3b, left panel), visual imprinting after two-hour training was not blocked by post-training administration of CHX (Figure 3b right panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Visual imprinting after two-hour training was not blocked by post-training administration of CHX.
source: While one-hour training triggered visual imprinting that was suppressed by CHX (Figure 3b, left panel), visual imprinting after two-hour training was not blocked by post-training administration of CHX (Figure 3b right panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: CHX effectively blocked imprinting-triggered protein synthesis in MNM.
source: Consistent with the effect on behavior, CHX effectively blocked imprinting-triggered protein synthesis in both MNM and IMM areas (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: CHX effectively blocked imprinting-triggered protein synthesis in IMM.
source: Consistent with the effect on behavior, CHX effectively blocked imprinting-triggered protein synthesis in both MNM and IMM areas (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Training significantly decreased p-eIF2α in the auditory area MNM.
source: Intriguingly, training significantly decreased p-eIF2α in the auditory area MNM (Figure 4a, left panel), but not in the visual area IMM (Figure 4a, right panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Training did not significantly decrease p-eIF2α in the visual area IMM.
source: Intriguingly, training significantly decreased p-eIF2α in the auditory area MNM (Figure 4a, left panel), but not in the visual area IMM (Figure 4a, right panel).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Sal003 increases p-eIF2α levels in chickens.
source: To examine whether a reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation is required for auditory imprinting we treated chickens before training with Sal003, an inhibitor of the eIF2α phosphatase complexes (McCamphill et al., 2015), which increases p-eIF2α levels (Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and decreases translation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sal003 decreases translation in chickens.
source: To examine whether a reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation is required for auditory imprinting we treated chickens before training with Sal003, an inhibitor of the eIF2α phosphatase complexes (McCamphill et al., 2015), which increases p-eIF2α levels (Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and decreases translation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing p-eIF2α with Sal003 prevented auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: Interestingly, increasing p-eIF2α with Sal003 prevented auditory imprinting, but had no effect on visual imprinting (Figure 4c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Sal003 had no effect on visual imprinting in chickens.
source: Interestingly, increasing p-eIF2α with Sal003 prevented auditory imprinting, but had no effect on visual imprinting (Figure 4c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: PKRi-injected chickens showed significantly stronger auditory imprinting compared to controls.
source: PKRi-injected chickens showed significantly stronger auditory imprinting compared to controls (Figure 4d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: PKRi failed to affect visual imprinting in chickens.
source: However, PKRi failed to affect visual imprinting (Figure 4d).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: ISRIB enhances translation in chickens.
source: To further demonstrate that auditory imprinting could be enhanced by reducing eIF2α-mediated translational control, chickens were injected with ISRIB, a compound that blocks the translational effects induced by p-eIF2α (Sidrauski et al., 2013) and increases translation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Injection of ISRIB immediately after training enhanced auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: Consistent with the PKRi-experiments, injection of ISRIB immediately after training enhanced auditory imprinting (Figure 4e) but not visual imprinting.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: ISRIB did not enhance visual imprinting in chickens.
source: Consistent with the PKRi-experiments, injection of ISRIB immediately after training enhanced auditory imprinting (Figure 4e) but not visual imprinting.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Plasticity in dendritic spines is thought to be crucial during critical periods.
source: Plasticity in dendritic spines, the major site of excitatory inputs in neurons, is thought to be crucial during CPs (Roberts et al., 2010) and part of the cellular substrate of memory (Lamprecht and LeDoux, 2004; Bourne and Harris, 2007; Nishiyama and Yasuda, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Roberts et al., 2010).

claim: Dendritic spines are the major site of excitatory inputs in neurons.
source: Plasticity in dendritic spines, the major site of excitatory inputs in neurons, is thought to be crucial during CPs (Roberts et al., 2010) and part of the cellular substrate of memory (Lamprecht and LeDoux, 2004; Bourne and Harris, 2007; Nishiyama and Yasuda, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Dendritic spine plasticity is part of the cellular substrate of memory.
source: Plasticity in dendritic spines, the major site of excitatory inputs in neurons, is thought to be crucial during CPs (Roberts et al., 2010) and part of the cellular substrate of memory (Lamprecht and LeDoux, 2004; Bourne and Harris, 2007; Nishiyama and Yasuda, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Lamprecht and LeDoux, 2004; Bourne and Harris, 2007; Nishiyama and Yasuda, 2015).

claim: Long-term remodeling of spines requires protein synthesis.
source: Given that (a) long-term remodeling of spines requires protein synthesis (Nishiyama and Yasuda, 2015) and (b) translational control by p-eIF2α selectively regulates auditory imprinting, we next examined the role of this translational control mechanism in structural plasticity in imprinting-relevant brain regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Nishiyama and Yasuda, 2015).

claim: Training failed to affect the total number of spines in MNM.
source: While training failed to affect the total number of spines (Figure 5d–e), it significantly increased the number of mushroom spines and decreased the number of thin spines in MNM (Figure 5d) and IMM (Figure 5e), compared to control animals with experience on the running wheel but not subject to audiovisual training.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Training failed to affect the total number of spines in IMM.
source: While training failed to affect the total number of spines (Figure 5d–e), it significantly increased the number of mushroom spines and decreased the number of thin spines in MNM (Figure 5d) and IMM (Figure 5e), compared to control animals with experience on the running wheel but not subject to audiovisual training.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Training significantly increased the number of mushroom spines in MNM.
source: While training failed to affect the total number of spines (Figure 5d–e), it significantly increased the number of mushroom spines and decreased the number of thin spines in MNM (Figure 5d) and IMM (Figure 5e), compared to control animals with experience on the running wheel but not subject to audiovisual training.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Training significantly decreased the number of thin spines in MNM.
source: While training failed to affect the total number of spines (Figure 5d–e), it significantly increased the number of mushroom spines and decreased the number of thin spines in MNM (Figure 5d) and IMM (Figure 5e), compared to control animals with experience on the running wheel but not subject to audiovisual training.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Training significantly increased the number of mushroom spines in IMM.
source: While training failed to affect the total number of spines (Figure 5d–e), it significantly increased the number of mushroom spines and decreased the number of thin spines in MNM (Figure 5d) and IMM (Figure 5e), compared to control animals with experience on the running wheel but not subject to audiovisual training.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Training significantly decreased the number of thin spines in IMM.
source: While training failed to affect the total number of spines (Figure 5d–e), it significantly increased the number of mushroom spines and decreased the number of thin spines in MNM (Figure 5d) and IMM (Figure 5e), compared to control animals with experience on the running wheel but not subject to audiovisual training.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Sal003 administration blocked the training-induced increase in the number of mushroom spines only in MNM.
source: Remarkably, Sal003 administration blocked the training-induced increase in the number of mushroom spines only in MNM (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d,e.

claim: Treatment with PKRi on P4 selectively re-opened the critical period for auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: Remarkably, treatment with either PKRi or ISRIB (Figure 6a) on P4 selectively re-opened the CP for auditory imprinting (Figure 6b), again without affecting visual imprinting (Figure 6c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Treatment with ISRIB on P4 selectively re-opened the critical period for auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: Remarkably, treatment with either PKRi or ISRIB (Figure 6a) on P4 selectively re-opened the CP for auditory imprinting (Figure 6b), again without affecting visual imprinting (Figure 6c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Treatment with PKRi on P4 did not affect visual imprinting in chickens.
source: Remarkably, treatment with either PKRi or ISRIB (Figure 6a) on P4 selectively re-opened the CP for auditory imprinting (Figure 6b), again without affecting visual imprinting (Figure 6c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Treatment with ISRIB on P4 did not affect visual imprinting in chickens.
source: Remarkably, treatment with either PKRi or ISRIB (Figure 6a) on P4 selectively re-opened the CP for auditory imprinting (Figure 6b), again without affecting visual imprinting (Figure 6c).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: eIF2α-mediated translational control exclusively regulated spine remodeling in the auditory but not in the visual area.
source: Furthermore, and consistent with our behavioral results, eIF2α-mediated translation exclusively regulated spine remodeling in the auditory but not in the visual area.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data on spine remodeling in MNM and IMM.

claim: Experience-dependent structural plasticity of dendritic spines requires eIF2α dephosphorylation.
source: While previous studies in adult rodents suggest that eIF2α-mediated translation regulates the two major forms of synaptic plasticity (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2011; Stern et al., 2013), here we report for the first time that experience-dependent structural plasticity of dendritic spines requires eIF2a dephosphorylation.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data on spine remodeling and eIF2α phosphorylation.

claim: Reducing p-eIF2α-mediated translational control in the VTA can convert adult into adolescent mice with respect to their vulnerability to cocaine-induced changes in synaptic strength and behavior.
source: A recent report shows that reducing p-eIF2α-mediated translational control in the VTA can convert adult into adolescent mice with respect to their vulnerability to cocaine-induced changes in synaptic strength and behavior (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Huang et al., 2016).

claim: Chickens are able to eat and drink water in the dark.
source: It has been shown that chickens are able to eat and drink water in the dark and that this housing does not impact visual acuity or locomotion, compared to chickens reared under light conditions(Yamaguchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Yamaguchi et al., 2012).

claim: Dark housing does not impact visual acuity or locomotion in chickens, compared to chickens reared under light conditions.
source: It has been shown that chickens are able to eat and drink water in the dark and that this housing does not impact visual acuity or locomotion, compared to chickens reared under light conditions(Yamaguchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Yamaguchi et al., 2012).

claim: IP-injected puromycin accessed the chicken's brain within 3–4 hr.
source: Because brain tissue incorporates PMY more slowly compared to other tissues (Flexner et al., 1962) pilot experiments were conducted, showing that IP-injected PMY accessed the chicken's brain within 3–4 hr.
evidence: This statement is supported by pilot experiments conducted by the authors.

claim: Brain tissue incorporates puromycin more slowly compared to other tissues.
source: Because brain tissue incorporates PMY more slowly compared to other tissues (Flexner et al., 1962) pilot experiments were conducted, showing that IP-injected PMY accessed the chicken's brain within 3–4 hr.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Flexner et al., 1962).

claim: Restoring translational control of eIF2α holds the promise to rejuvenate adult brain plasticity and restore learning and memory in a variety of cognitive disorders.
source: Restoring translational control of eIF2α holds the promise to rejuvenate adult brain plasticity and restore learning and memory in a variety of cognitive disorders.
evidence: This statement is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Blocking p-eIF2α-mediated translational control could be used to recover plasticity in the mature brain and treat cognitive dysfunctions.
source: Based on these results and the evolutionarily conserved nature of this process, we speculate that reopening CPs through blockade of eIF2α-mediated translational control could be used to recover plasticity in the mature brain and treat cognitive dysfunctions.
evidence: This statement is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study and the evolutionarily conserved nature of the process.

claim: The translation of mRNA into protein occurs in three steps: initiation, elongation and termination.
source: The translation of mRNA into protein occurs in three steps: initiation, elongation and termination and can be regulated through several signaling pathways (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in molecular biology and a citation to previous literature (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).

claim: Translation can be regulated through several signaling pathways.
source: The translation of mRNA into protein occurs in three steps: initiation, elongation and termination and can be regulated through several signaling pathways (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).

claim: IMM is located 2.5 mm from the dorsal surface of the brain and 0.5–1 mm from the caudal edge of the forebrain, limited below and laterally by the lateral ventricle.
source: IMM is located 2.5 mm from the dorsal surface of the brain and 0.5–1 mm from the caudal edge of the forebrain, limited below and laterally by the lateral ventricle.
evidence: This statement describes the anatomical location of IMM based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: MNM is located 0.5–1 mm lateral from the midline, 3 mm from the dorsal surface of the brain and 5 mm from the caudal edge of the forebrain, below the lateral pallial lamina that separates the hyperpallium and mesopallium.
source: MNM is located 0.5–1 mm lateral from the midline, 3 mm from the dorsal surface of the brain and 5 mm from the caudal edge of the forebrain, below the lateral pallial lamina that separates the hyperpallium and mesopallium (Puelles et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement describes the anatomical location of MNM based on a citation to previous literature (Puelles et al., 2007).

claim: Sal003 is an inhibitor of the eIF2α phosphatase complexes.
source: To examine whether a reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation is required for auditory imprinting we treated chickens before training with Sal003, an inhibitor of the eIF2α phosphatase complexes (McCamphill et al., 2015), which increases p-eIF2α levels (Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and decreases translation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (McCamphill et al., 2015).

claim: ISRIB is a compound that blocks the translational effects induced by p-eIF2α.
source: To further demonstrate that auditory imprinting could be enhanced by reducing eIF2α-mediated translational control, chickens were injected with ISRIB, a compound that blocks the translational effects induced by p-eIF2α (Sidrauski et al., 2013) and increases translation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Sidrauski et al., 2013).

claim: Spine classification based on head width, presence of neck and overall length is informative about the functionality and maturity of spines.
source: The spines 'head width, presence of neck and overall length were used for classifying them in filopodia, stubby, thin, or mushroom, using published criteria (Bourne and Harris, 2007; Sanders et al., 2012; Chakravarthy et al., 2006). Briefly, spines without clear head and neck, and shorter than 1 μm, were categorized as stubby. Spines longer than 1 μm were classified as mushroom or thin, depending on whether a head and neck were observed. Protrusions longer than 2 μm were categorized as filopodia.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Bourne and Harris, 2007; Sanders et al., 2012; Chakravarthy et al., 2006) describing the classification method.

claim: Decreasing p-eIF2α is required for auditory imprinting in chickens.
source: These results indicate that decreasing p-eIF2α is only required for auditory imprinting.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the experimental results showing that increasing p-eIF2α blocks auditory imprinting and decreasing p-eIF2α enhances it.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation controls imprinting behavior during the critical period.
source: Thus, our results shed light on the biological basis of experience-dependent spine remodeling and uncovered eIF2α as a major player in spine remodeling.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data showing that manipulating eIF2α phosphorylation affects imprinting behavior.

claim: eIF2α is a major player in experience-dependent spine remodeling.
source: Thus, our results shed light on the biological basis of experience-dependent spine remodeling and uncovered eIF2α as a major player in spine remodeling.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data showing that eIF2α phosphorylation regulates spine remodeling in MNM.

claim: Reducing p-eIF2α-mediated translational control enhances auditory imprinting by promoting brain plasticity.
source: Hence, by promoting brain plasticity, the reduction of p-eIF2α-mediated translational control enhances auditory imprinting.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the experimental results showing that reducing p-eIF2α enhances auditory imprinting and reopens the critical period.

claim: Reopening critical periods through blockade of eIF2α-mediated translational control is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism.
source: Based on these results and the evolutionarily conserved nature of this process, we speculate that reopening CPs through blockade of eIF2α-mediated translational control could be used to recover plasticity in the mature brain and treat cognitive dysfunctions.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the findings in chickens and previous studies in rodents showing similar mechanisms.

claim: The structural plasticity found in IMM and MNM could be consistent with potentiation and enlargement of specific dendritic spines, favoring the detection of imprinted stimuli.
source: In this case, the structural plasticity found in IMM and MNM could be consistent with potentiation and enlargement of specific dendritic spines, favoring the detection of imprinted stimuli.
evidence: This statement is a speculative interpretation of the observed structural plasticity data.

claim: The increase in mushroom spines and decrease in thin spines may suggest coordinated structural plasticity.
source: While we did not observe changes in spine density, the increase in mushroom spines and decrease in thin spines may suggest coordinated structural plasticity as previously reported in hippocampal slices (Bourne and Harris, 2011).
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the observed data and comparison to previous studies (Bourne and Harris, 2011).

claim: Glutamate application induces a transient increase of eIF2α phosphorylation in glial cells in vitro.
source: Glutamate application induces a transient increase of eIF2α phosphorylation in glial cells in vitro (Flores-Méndez et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Flores-Méndez et al., 2013).

claim: The transient increase of eIF2α phosphorylation in glial cells has been linked to glutamate removal from the synaptic cleft by glial cells.
source: This effect has been linked to glutamate removal from the synaptic cleft by glial cells (Flores-Méndez et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature (Flores-Méndez et al., 2013).

claim: Releasing 'epigenetic brakes' could reopen auditory critical periods in mice and humans.
source: Moreover, in mice and humans, releasing 'epigenetic brakes', could reopen auditory CPs (Yang et al., 2012; Gervain et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Yang et al., 2012; Gervain et al., 2013).

claim: Direct manipulation of inhibitory synaptic transmission can reactivate plasticity in the visual cortex of rodents after critical periods are closed.
source: This has been successfully achieved in the visual cortex of rodents through direct manipulation of inhibitory synaptic transmission, either pharmacologically (Hensch et al., 1998) or through transplantation of embryonic inhibitory neurons (Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature (Hensch et al., 1998; Davis et al., 2015).

claim: Behavioral training decreases p-eIF2α in chickens.
source: Given that (a) behavioral training decreases p-eIF2α (Figure 4a), (b) blocking p-eIF2α-mediated translation enhances auditory imprinting elicited by weak-training protocol (Figure 4d–e) and (c) Sal003-mediated increase in p-eIF2α blocks auditory imprinting, we wondered whether the drugs enhancing imprinting during the CP (PKRi and ISRIB) would restore imprinting outside the CP (Figure 6a).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Blocking p-eIF2α-mediated translation enhances auditory imprinting elicited by weak-training protocol.
source: Given that (a) behavioral training decreases p-eIF2α (Figure 4a), (b) blocking p-eIF2α-mediated translation enhances auditory imprinting elicited by weak-training protocol (Figure 4d–e) and (c) Sal003-mediated increase in p-eIF2α blocks auditory imprinting, we wondered whether the drugs enhancing imprinting during the CP (PKRi and ISRIB) would restore imprinting outside the CP (Figure 6a).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: Sal003-mediated increase in p-eIF2α blocks auditory imprinting.
source: Given that (a) behavioral training decreases p-eIF2α (Figure 4a), (b) blocking p-eIF2α-mediated translation enhances auditory imprinting elicited by weak-training protocol (Figure 4d–e) and (c) Sal003-mediated increase in p-eIF2α blocks auditory imprinting, we wondered whether the drugs enhancing imprinting during the CP (PKRi and ISRIB) would restore imprinting outside the CP (Figure 6a).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data showing that Sal003 blocks auditory imprinting.

claim: The reason why eIF2α is not involved in visual imprinting is not yet understood.
source: The reason why eIF2α is not involved in visual imprinting is not yet understood.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in understanding based on the experimental findings.

claim: Expression of eIF2α kinase or phosphatase complexes may differ between visual and auditory areas.
source: It is possible that expression of eIF2α kinase or phosphatase complexes differs between visual and auditory areas, or that upstream signaling pathways fail to engage eIF2α dephosphorylation.
evidence: This statement is a speculative explanation for the observed differences between auditory and visual imprinting.

claim: Upstream signaling pathways may fail to engage eIF2α dephosphorylation in visual imprinting.
source: It is possible that expression of eIF2α kinase or phosphatase complexes differs between visual and auditory areas, or that upstream signaling pathways fail to engage eIF2α dephosphorylation.
evidence: This statement is a speculative explanation for the observed differences between auditory and visual imprinting.

claim: Other translational control pathways such as those controlled by mTORC1 may mediate the formation of visual memories.
source: An appealing idea is that other translational control pathways such those controlled by the mechanistic target of rapamycin mTORC1 (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009) mediate the formation of visual memories.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings and knowledge of other translational control pathways.
